case_analysis.focal_point: Whether restitution mandated by the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act is a criminal punishment such that retroactive application triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 (Ex Post Facto Clause) as applied to restitution orders under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 (MVRA), Pub. L. No. 104-132, 110 Stat. 1227.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that MVRA restitution is penal in nature because it is imposed as part of a criminal sentence, is mandatory for covered offenses, is enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms, and serves classic punishment goals (retribution and deterrence) in addition to compensation; therefore, treating it as non-punitive would permit retroactive increases in a defendant’s sentence and undermine the Ex Post Facto Clause’s core bar on heightened punishment after the fact.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States’ litigating position evolved: in its certiorari-stage opposition it argued the Eighth Circuit’s judgment should be affirmed because, even assuming MVRA restitution is punishment, the particular retroactive application at issue did not increase punishment (so no ex post facto violation). After cert was granted, the Solicitor General notified the Court it would not defend the Eighth Circuit’s rationale and would instead support petitioner on the limited question presented—indicating agreement (or at least non-opposition) that MVRA restitution should be treated as criminal punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes and urging vacatur rather than affirmance on the lower court’s reasoning.

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that restitution is compensatory and thus “civil,” but under Hudson/Ward we begin with Congress’s design, and the MVRA is embedded in the criminal sentencing framework—mandatory upon conviction, imposed at sentencing, and entered in the criminal judgment “in addition to … any other penalty.” Justice Thomas’s emphasis on that structural choice is decisive absent the “clearest proof” that the scheme is in fact civil, and the compensatory destination of funds to victims does not supply that proof. Justice Kagan’s workability concern reinforces the institutional stakes: if we treat this sentencing component as nonpunitive, legislatures could retroactively increase burdens attached to criminal judgments by relabeling them “compensation,” diluting the Ex Post Facto Clause. A narrow holding confined to MVRA restitution imposed as part of the criminal sentence (without opining on other restitution regimes) best respects precedent and preserves institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that restitution is compensatory and thus “civil”—cannot overcome the MVRA’s text and structure, which make restitution a mandatory component of the criminal sentence imposed at sentencing and entered in the criminal judgment. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, accepting a civil-label theory here would invite evasion of the Ex Post Facto Clause by retroactively increasing sentencing consequences under the guise of “compensation,” an outcome inconsistent with the Clause’s original public meaning as a restraint on after-the-fact punishment increases. Hudson/Ward instruct us to begin with Congress’s chosen mechanism and depart only on the “clearest proof,” and nothing about victim payment supplies that proof when Congress has embedded the sanction in Title 18 sentencing procedures “in addition to … any other penalty.” Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on the MVRA’s “to the extent constitutionally permissible” proviso reinforces that Congress anticipated constitutional limits on retroactivity rather than silently authorizing it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best claim—that MVRA restitution is merely compensatory and therefore civil—cannot overcome the statute’s text and sentencing-centered structure: restitution is imposed “in addition to … any other penalty,” ordered at sentencing, and entered in the criminal judgment, which under Hudson/Ward is powerful evidence of punitive design absent the “clearest proof” to the contrary. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on Congress’s deliberate choice of Title 18 criminal machinery and mandatory, conviction-triggered imposition is decisive on a textualist analysis, and no one has offered a precedent that truly permits reclassifying this component of a criminal sentence as nonpunitive simply because victims receive payment. Chief Justice Roberts’s workability point reinforces the practical stakes: if we accept a compensatory label here, legislatures could retroactively increase sentencing burdens by semantic relabeling, eroding the Ex Post Facto Clause’s core constraint. Even if we proceeded to Mendoza-Martinez, the obligation’s mandatory, offense-specific, sentencing-based operation and enforcement mechanisms have sufficient punitive effect to trigger ex post facto scrutiny.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that MVRA restitution is compensatory and thus “civil”—cannot overcome the statute’s operation: it is mandatory upon conviction, imposed at sentencing, and entered “in addition to any other penalty,” making it function as an added sentencing consequence. Chief Justice Roberts is right that accepting a civil label here would invite a straightforward end-run around the Ex Post Facto Clause by retroactively increasing burdens in the criminal judgment. Justice Thomas’s Hudson/Ward framing also matters: Congress chose the criminal sentencing mechanism, and there is no “clearest proof” that the scheme is so nonpunitive in effect that we should recharacterize it, especially given its deterrent/retributive features that fall hardest on indigent defendants. Congress’s “to the extent constitutionally permissible” proviso underscores that retroactivity must yield where it increases punishment, and this does.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The best respondent argument remains that MVRA restitution is compensatory and therefore outside the Ex Post Facto Clause, but the statute’s text and design make it part of the criminal sentence: it is imposed at sentencing, entered in the criminal judgment, and mandated for covered offenses. Chief Justice Roberts’s workability concern is decisive for me—if we accept a “compensation” label to avoid ex post facto scrutiny, Congress could retroactively increase sentencing consequences simply by redirecting payments to victims, undermining a core constitutional constraint. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Pasquantino strengthens the point that our precedents have treated restitution in the criminal case as penal in relevant respects, making the respondent’s civil-only characterization hard to sustain under Hudson/Ward and Smith v. Doe’s intent-effects framework. A narrow holding limited to MVRA restitution ordered through the criminal judgment preserves statutory coherence and avoids overreaching into other restitution regimes.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that restitution is compensatory, but under Hudson/Ward we start with Congress’s design, and here the MVRA is imposed at sentencing “in addition to… any other penalty” and entered/enforced as part of the criminal judgment—features that are difficult to square with a purely civil remedy absent the “clearest proof.” Justice Thomas’s emphasis on statutory structure (Title 18 placement, conviction-triggered mandate, sentencing procedures) reinforces that we need not (and should not) reclassify a component of a criminal sentence based on its beneficiary. Even if we reached Mendoza-Martinez, the mandatory, offense-specific, conviction-triggered obligation has deterrent and retributive effects, making retroactive application an increase in punishment in the Ex Post Facto sense. I also share Chief Justice Roberts’s view that we should write narrowly to MVRA restitution as part of the criminal sentence, leaving other restitution regimes for another day.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that restitution is compensatory and thus “civil,” but Hudson/Ward require us to start with Congress’s design choice, and the MVRA’s placement in Title 18, its “in addition to any other penalty” language, and its imposition at sentencing as part of the criminal judgment make that civil characterization hard to sustain absent the “clearest proof.” Chief Justice Roberts’s legitimacy/workability concern is persuasive under an institutionalist approach: if we bless retroactive mandatory restitution as nonpunitive, we effectively authorize retroactive sentence enhancements by relabeling sentencing components as compensation, weakening the Ex Post Facto Clause. Justice Thomas’s structural argument further reinforces that we need not overextend Mendoza-Martinez when the statute’s form is plainly criminal, and any mixed compensatory purpose doesn’t negate the punitive mechanism and effects. A narrow holding—MVRA restitution imposed as part of the criminal sentence counts as punishment for ex post facto purposes—fits precedent and preserves administrability without opining on other restitution schemes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that restitution is compensatory and paid to victims, but under Ward and Hudson we start with Congress’s chosen mechanism, and the MVRA is textually and structurally part of the criminal sentence (ordered at sentencing, entered in the criminal judgment, and imposed “in addition to … any other penalty”). Justice Thomas’s emphasis on Title 18 placement and § 3556’s sentencing integration underscores that we lack the “clearest proof” required to recharacterize this sanction as civil for Ex Post Facto purposes. Justice Kagan’s citation to Pasquantino further supports treating restitution as penal in relevant contexts, weakening any attempt to treat MVRA restitution as merely a freestanding compensatory remedy. Even if we reached Mendoza-Martinez, the conviction-triggered, mandatory, offense-specific obligation—administered through criminal enforcement channels—has sufficiently punitive form and effect that retroactive increases would be unconstitutional.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—compensation plus Hudson/Ward deference to a civil label—still collapses under the MVRA’s actual design and operation: it is conviction-triggered, mandatory, imposed at sentencing, and enforced through the criminal judgment, so it functions as a sentencing consequence for Ex Post Facto purposes. Chief Justice Roberts’s workability concern is decisive for me as a pragmatic matter: if we accept a “compensatory” label here, legislatures could retroactively increase the burdens of a criminal sentence by rebranding punishment as restitution, hollowing out the Clause. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Pasquantino further undercuts respondent’s civil-only framing by showing our precedents have treated restitution ordered in the criminal case as penal in character. On my procedural-fairness lens, retroactive mandatory restitution—especially with criminal enforcement tools—operates like increased punishment after the fact, and that is the constitutional harm the Ex Post Facto Clause is meant to prevent.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause bars laws that retroactively increase criminal punishment, and under Hudson v. United States and Ward the inquiry turns first on statutory construction and congressional intent, with departure from that intent only on the “clearest proof.” The MVRA operates as part of the criminal judgment—mandated at sentencing for specified offenses and enforced through criminal-sentence mechanisms—so it is best understood as a penal consequence rather than a freestanding civil remedy, bringing it within Art. I, § 9, cl. 3. Treating MVRA restitution as nonpunitive would invite retroactive increases to a defendant’s sentence and risk undermining the Clause’s core function and the Court’s institutional legitimacy by permitting end-runs around settled ex post facto constraints. A narrow holding recognizing MVRA restitution as punishment for ex post facto purposes resolves the question presented without unnecessary pronouncements about restitution in other statutory settings.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause forbids retroactive increases in criminal punishment, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, and the MVRA’s text and structure show Congress made restitution part of the criminal sentence: it is codified in Title 18, imposed "in addition to . . . any other penalty," and ordered at sentencing through criminal-judgment mechanisms, 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A(a)(1), 3556. Under Hudson v. United States, 522 U.S. 93 (1997), the threshold question is whether the legislature indicated a preference for a civil or criminal mechanism; here, Congress plainly selected the criminal one, so the analysis need not proceed to the second-step factors. This Court has likewise described restitution as a penal sanction imposed as part of a criminal conviction and sentence, see Pasquantino v. United States, 544 U.S. 349, 365 (2005), reinforcing that retroactive application would trigger ex post facto scrutiny. Accordingly, MVRA restitution should be treated as punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes, and its retroactive application is constitutionally suspect.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The MVRA’s restitution scheme is imposed as part of the criminal judgment and sentence, is mandatory for covered offenses, and is administered through criminal procedures; that structure strongly indicates Congress intended it to operate as a penal sanction, bringing it within the Ex Post Facto Clause of U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3. Under Hudson v. United States, 522 U.S. 93, 99 (1997), and United States v. Ward, 448 U.S. 242, 248–51 (1980), the inquiry begins with statutory construction and gives primacy to legislative intent, and here the MVRA’s placement and operation in the criminal sentencing framework point to punishment rather than a purely civil remedy. Even if one proceeds to the Mendoza-Martinez factors, the mandatory, offense-triggered obligation imposed at sentencing and enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms has sufficiently punitive purpose and effect to be treated as criminal for ex post facto purposes. Treating MVRA restitution as nonpunitive would invite retroactive increases in the burdens imposed at sentencing, a result the Ex Post Facto Clause is designed to prevent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Restitution under the MVRA is imposed as part of the criminal judgment, is mandatory for covered offenses, and is enforced through criminal-sentencing mechanisms, all of which strongly indicate it functions as punishment notwithstanding its compensatory features. Applying the Mendoza-Martinez purpose-and-effects factors, MVRA restitution advances traditional punitive aims like deterrence and retribution and applies only upon conviction for criminal conduct, making retroactive application constitutionally suspect under the Ex Post Facto Clause, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3. While Congress included a retroactivity provision in MVRA § 211 ("to the extent constitutionally permissible"), that language cannot authorize retroactive increases in the penal consequences of past conduct. Given the real-world impact of enlarging financial penalties after the fact—especially on indigent defendants and their families—the Constitution requires treating MVRA restitution as criminal punishment for ex post facto purposes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Applying the Mendoza-Martinez framework as reiterated in Smith v. Doe, MVRA restitution is imposed in the criminal judgment as part of the sentence, is mandatory for covered offenses, and is enforced through criminal mechanisms, all of which strongly indicate punitive form and effect even if Congress also sought victim compensation. The statute’s placement and operation under 18 U.S.C. § 3663A make restitution function like a sentencing consequence rather than a freestanding civil remedy, and treating it otherwise would permit retroactive increases in a defendant’s sentence contrary to the Ex Post Facto Clause, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3. Given the workability and coherence concerns, the better rule is that MVRA restitution counts as “punishment” for ex post facto purposes, leaving case-specific disputes about whether a particular retroactive change increases the amount or duration of liability for application on remand. This approach aligns with the Court’s punitive-effects analysis and avoids the administratively awkward line-drawing that would follow from characterizing criminal-judgment restitution as purely civil.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause bars retroactive increases in criminal punishment, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, and MVRA restitution is imposed as part of the criminal judgment and sentence, not as a freestanding civil remedy. Applying the Mendoza-Martinez framework as this Court reiterated in Smith v. Doe, the MVRA’s mandatory, offense-triggered imposition through criminal sentencing procedures and its deterrent/retributive features make restitution sufficiently punitive in form and effect to be treated as punishment for ex post facto purposes. Accepting the Eighth Circuit’s civil-labeling would permit Congress to enlarge sentencing consequences after the fact by rebranding penalties as “compensation,” eroding a core separation-of-powers constraint on retrospective lawmaking. At minimum, where the statute’s operation functions as a sentencing consequence, the Constitution requires treating it as punishment to prevent retroactive aggravation of the defendant’s legal consequences.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: For Ex Post Facto purposes, the threshold question is whether Congress made the sanction part of the criminal law; that inquiry is “at least initially, a matter of statutory construction.” Hudson v. United States, 522 U.S. 93, 99 (1997). The MVRA operates through the criminal judgment, is imposed at sentencing, and is mandatory for covered offenses, which strongly indicates Congress labeled and intended it as a criminal sanction rather than a freestanding civil remedy, making the Ex Post Facto Clause applicable under U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3. Even if Congress’s intent were characterized as compensatory, the enforcement mechanisms and mandatory, offense-triggered character provide substantial evidence that restitution is sufficiently punitive in effect to satisfy the Smith v. Doe / Mendoza-Martinez framework. Treating MVRA restitution as non-punitive would create serious practical and legitimacy concerns by allowing retroactive increases in criminal sentences, contrary to the Clause’s core purpose.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause bars laws that retroactively increase “punishment,” and the MVRA’s text and structure strongly indicate restitution is imposed as part of the criminal sentence: it is mandatory for covered offenses, ordered at sentencing, and governed by criminal-sentencing procedures. See 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A, 3664(c) (incorporating Fed. R. Crim. P. 32), which aligns restitution with traditional penal sanctions rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Under the Mendoza-Martinez/Hudson framework, even if Congress used the compensatory label “restitution,” the use of quintessential criminal procedures and its operation within the criminal judgment provide substantial evidence of punitive character for constitutional classification. See Hudson v. United States, 522 U.S. 93, 103 (1997) (procedural design is probative of civil vs. criminal sanction).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: For Ex Post Facto purposes, the proper inquiry is the two-step intent-effects framework of Kennedy v. Mendoza-Martinez, as applied in Smith v. Doe, 538 U.S. 84, 92-97 (2003). Although Congress may have described MVRA restitution in compensatory terms, its operation is inseparable from the criminal judgment: it is imposed at sentencing, is mandatory for covered offenses, and is enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms—features that, in practical effect, make it function like an added component of the defendant’s sentence. Given the Clause’s core prohibition on retroactively increasing punishment, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, and the real-world consequences for defendants’ liberty and financial obligations, I would treat MVRA restitution as sufficiently punitive in effect to trigger Ex Post Facto scrutiny when applied retroactively.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether restitution imposed under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act is a criminal punishment such that applying it (or an MVRA amendment) retroactively triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 (Ex Post Facto Clause) as applied to restitution ordered under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 (MVRA), Pub. L. No. 104-132, tit. II, subtit. A, 110 Stat. 1227.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that MVRA restitution is penal in nature because it is imposed as part of the criminal sentence, is mandatory for covered offenses, is enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, and serves traditional punishment goals (deterrence, retribution, and incapacitation via supervision and collection tools). Therefore, when Congress later changes restitution rules in a way that increases a defendant’s restitution exposure and courts apply that change to pre-enactment conduct, it retroactively increases punishment and violates the Ex Post Facto Clause. Petitioner and amici also emphasize that although labeled 'restitution,' MVRA awards can diverge from ordinary civil compensation concepts and operate like a monetary penalty attached to conviction.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government’s position evolved across the filings: (1) in its brief in opposition, it defended affirmance on the ground that—even assuming MVRA restitution is punishment—there was no ex post facto violation because the challenged retroactive application did not increase punishment in the relevant way; (2) after cert was granted, the Solicitor General notified the Court the government would not defend the Eighth Circuit’s rationale and would support petitioner on the question presented; and (3) in its merits brief supporting vacatur, the government agrees the Court should resolve the limited question whether MVRA restitution is criminal punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes (and supports vacatur consistent with that view), rather than relying on the Eighth Circuit’s contrary rationale.
key_precedents: The materials provided do not quote or list specific Supreme Court precedent by name; they primarily frame the dispute around the Ex Post Facto Clause and the penal/non-penal characterization of MVRA restitution.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—the Hudson/Smith “clearest proof” hurdle coupled with Congress’s compensatory label—does not, in my view, defeat the claim here because the relevant effects are unusually sentence-like: MVRA restitution is imposed only upon conviction, entered in the criminal judgment, and enforced through mechanisms tightly linked to sentencing, which under Mendoza-Martinez supplies the needed proof when an amendment retroactively increases the amount owed. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline matters for my analysis not as dispositive holdings, but because those cases reflect our own repeated description of restitution as a criminal penalty imposed at sentencing, making it harder to treat a retroactive increase as purely civil adjustment. At the same time, I share Alito’s administrability concern, which is why I would keep the holding narrow—limited to retroactive statutory amendments that increase a defendant’s mandatory restitution exposure for pre-enactment conduct—so we do not constitutionalize routine collection or payment modifications under § 3664. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning framing reinforces the anti-evasion principle, but I would rest the opinion on our intent-effects framework and the statute’s operation rather than a categorical historical rule that could sweep too broadly.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that Hudson/Smith’s “clearest proof” and Congress’s compensatory label should control—fails under the Constitution’s original public meaning of “punishment,” which included mandatory pecuniary sanctions imposed by reason of a criminal conviction and enforced through penal processes. The MVRA’s operative features (conviction-triggered, mandatory, entered in the criminal judgment, and enforced through sentencing-linked mechanisms) supply the very “effects” that Hudson/Mendoza-Martinez treat as punitive, and Chief Justice Roberts is right that accepting mere relabeling would invite evasion of the Ex Post Facto Clause. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline, while not Ex Post Facto holdings, is still probative because it confirms our consistent description of restitution as a criminal penalty imposed at sentencing, supporting the conclusion that retroactively increasing restitution exposure increases punishment. A narrow rule—limited to retroactive amendments that increase mandatory restitution liability tied to conviction—answers Alito’s administrability concern without abandoning the Clause’s original constraint on retroactive penal consequences.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s points about restitution’s placement in the criminal judgment and its conviction-triggered, mandatory character are the most substantial evidence of punitive “form,” and they sharpen the concern about legislative relabeling. But under Hudson and Smith v. Doe, the question is not whether the obligation is sentence-adjacent; it is whether its effects are so punitive as to overcome Congress’s remedial design by the “clearest proof,” and a loss-capped, victim-directed payment (with § 3664’s adjustment and collection features) still looks materially different from a fine calibrated to blameworthiness. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline does not move the constitutional needle for me because those “penalty” characterizations were not Ex Post Facto holdings and do not displace the intent-effects framework that tolerates mixed deterrent/retributive overtones absent overwhelming punitive effect. I remain concerned that adopting the Petitioner’s rule—even if labeled “narrow”—will invite ex post facto challenges to routine restitution-related amendments and impede victim compensation without a clearer constitutional command.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—the Hudson/Smith “clearest proof” hurdle given Congress’s compensatory label and loss-based calibration—does not defeat the ex post facto claim because the MVRA’s form and effects supply that proof: restitution is mandatory upon conviction, imposed at sentencing, and entered/enforced as part of a criminal judgment, which are classic punishment markers under Mendoza-Martinez. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline matters to my analysis because it reflects this Court’s repeated understanding of criminal restitution as a sentencing “penalty,” reinforcing that retroactively enlarging the amount owed increases punishment in the real-world sense that the Ex Post Facto Clause targets. And even accepting the compensatory aim, Chief Justice Roberts is right that letting Congress evade ex post facto limits by relabeling conviction-triggered financial sanctions would hollow the Clause’s protection. Given the coercive consequences for indigent defendants in particular, I remain persuaded that retroactive MVRA amendments increasing restitution exposure are constitutionally punitive.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Hudson/Smith “clearest proof” point is the best counter, but I think the MVRA’s text and operational design supply that proof: restitution is triggered only upon conviction, is mandatory for covered crimes, and is imposed and enforced through the sentencing judgment—features that make it function as a penal consequence when retroactively increased. Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability/evasion concern matters to my pragmatic textualism: if Congress can enlarge conviction-linked financial exposure after the fact simply by calling it “restitution,” the Ex Post Facto constraint becomes too easy to circumvent. Justice Jackson’s invocation of Pasquantino and Paroline doesn’t control the doctrinal test, but it is relevant evidence that our cases repeatedly describe criminal restitution as a “penalty” imposed at sentencing, which coheres with treating retroactive increases as increases in punishment. I would keep the holding narrow—limited to retroactive amendments that increase mandatory restitution exposure for pre-enactment conduct—addressing Alito’s fear of constitutionalizing all restitution administration.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Hudson/Smith “clearest proof” point is the best argument for respondent, but the MVRA’s text and operation supply that proof: it is conviction-triggered, mandatory, imposed in the sentencing judgment, and enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms—features that, under Mendoza-Martinez, are quintessentially punitive in effect even if Congress uses compensatory labels. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning framing reinforces that mandatory pecuniary exactions imposed by reason of conviction were understood as punishment, and allowing Congress to avoid the Ex Post Facto Clause by relabeling such sanctions “restitution” would defeat the Clause’s structural purpose. Justice Jackson’s citations to Pasquantino and Paroline matter because they confirm our own repeated characterization of criminal restitution as a sentencing “penalty,” undermining the claim that it is merely a civil remedy for Article I purposes. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow approach addresses administrability: we need only hold that retroactive amendments increasing MVRA restitution exposure increase punishment, not constitutionalize all restitution administration.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point remains Hudson/Smith’s “clearest proof” requirement and Congress’s compensatory labeling, but I think the MVRA’s design and real-world operation supply that proof when a later amendment retroactively increases the amount a defendant must pay: it is triggered only by conviction, imposed through sentencing, entered in the criminal judgment, and enforced through the criminal-justice apparatus. Chief Justice Roberts’s institutionalist framing is persuasive to me because it narrows the rule to retroactive increases in sentence-linked restitution exposure, answering Alito’s administrability concern without turning every restitution collection tweak into an ex post facto event. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline matters as confirmation that our cases repeatedly treat criminal restitution as a penalty imposed as part of the sentence—while not dispositive, it undercuts the claim that this is merely a civil remedial device for Article I purposes. Under a precedent- and tradition-focused approach, allowing Congress to evade ex post facto limits by relabeling conviction-triggered monetary penalties as “restitution” would be inconsistent with the Clause’s function and our intent-effects framework as applied to this mandatory, sentence-integrated sanction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—the Hudson/Smith “clearest proof” hurdle and Congress’s compensatory labeling—does not carry the day because the Ex Post Facto inquiry turns on how the statute operates, not its caption. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, MVRA restitution is mandatory, conviction-triggered, incorporated into the criminal judgment, and enforced through sentencing-linked mechanisms, which supplies the “clearest proof” that its effects are punitive under Mendoza-Martinez when an amendment retroactively increases exposure. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline, while not ex post facto holdings, matters because those cases describe restitution as a criminal penalty imposed at sentencing—confirming that, in our own vocabulary, it functions as part of punishment rather than a freestanding civil remedy. A narrow rule limited to retroactive increases in mandatory restitution liability avoids Alito’s administrability concern while preventing Congress from evading Article I, § 9 by relabeling monetary punishment as “restitution.”

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest argument—that Hudson/Smith requires “clearest proof” to override Congress’s compensatory intent and that the MVRA’s loss-based design keeps it civil—does not survive a pragmatic, effects-focused look at how the scheme actually operates. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, MVRA restitution is triggered only by conviction, imposed as part of the criminal sentence, and enforced through the criminal judgment’s coercive machinery, which under Mendoza-Martinez makes a retroactive increase function like an increase in punishment even if it also compensates. Justice Sotomayor’s point about real-world coercive consequences for indigent defendants reinforces that the amendment meaningfully enlarges defendants’ sentencing exposure after the fact in a way the Ex Post Facto Clause is designed to prevent. Pasquantino/Paroline are not controlling holdings on ex post facto, but they do undercut Alito’s “purely remedial” characterization by reflecting this Court’s repeated understanding that restitution is a criminal penalty imposed at sentencing.

John Roberts.reasoning: Applying the Mendoza-Martinez intent-effects framework, as reaffirmed in Smith v. Doe, 538 U.S. 84, 92-97 (2003), MVRA restitution is imposed as part of the criminal judgment and enforced through criminal sentencing mechanisms, which strongly indicates a punitive effect even if Congress used compensatory labels. Given the Ex Post Facto Clause, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, we should avoid a rule that would permit Congress to increase a defendant’s restitution exposure after the offense by relabeling monetary punishment as “restitution.” A narrow holding is appropriate: restitution under the MVRA operates as criminal punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes when an amendment retroactively increases the defendant’s financial liability tied to conviction. That approach aligns with institutional legitimacy by applying a settled test and preventing retroactive increases in the penal consequences of crime.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause forbids Congress from retroactively increasing “punishment” for past conduct, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, and restitution under the MVRA is imposed only upon conviction and as part of the criminal judgment and sentence, 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A, 3664. Applying the text and original public meaning of “punishment,” a mandatory monetary sanction triggered by a public offense and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms is penal in nature, even if it also compensates victims. Under Hudson v. United States and the Mendoza-Martinez factors, MVRA restitution is affirmative and burdensome, historically akin to pecuniary penalties attached to conviction, and serves deterrent and retributive aims, making its retroactive increase constitutionally suspect. Therefore, an MVRA amendment that increases restitution exposure cannot be applied to pre-enactment conduct without violating the Ex Post Facto Clause.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying the two-step Mendoza-Martinez framework as reiterated in Smith v. Doe, the MVRA’s restitution scheme is best understood as a compensatory mechanism for victims rather than a criminal punishment that triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause. Congress labeled the remedy “restitution,” keyed it to the victim’s actual loss, and provided collection and adjustment procedures in 18 U.S.C. § 3664 (including modification under § 3664(k)), all of which point to a remedial purpose rather than retribution. Even if imposed in a criminal judgment, the question is whether the measure is “so punitive in form and effect” as to override the civil intent, and the MVRA’s structure does not meet that demanding standard. Practical consequences also counsel against constitutionalizing routine restitution administration and amendments as “punishment,” which would impede effective victim compensation without clear textual command from Article I, § 9, cl. 3.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: MVRA restitution is imposed through quintessential criminal-sentencing procedures and as part of the judgment of conviction, see 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A, 3664(c), which strongly indicates a punitive sanction when assessed under the Mendoza-Martinez framework as applied in Smith v. Doe, 538 U.S. 84, 92–97 (2003). Unlike the administrative penalties in Hudson v. United States, 522 U.S. 93, 103 (1997), MVRA restitution is mandatory for covered offenses and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, making it function in form and effect like punishment rather than a purely civil compensatory remedy. Because it operates as a component of the criminal sentence, applying an MVRA change retroactively that increases a defendant’s restitution exposure increases punishment and triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3. This conclusion also best protects fairness for defendants—often indigent—who are uniquely vulnerable to the coercive consequences of retroactively enhanced criminal financial obligations.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Restitution under the MVRA is imposed only upon conviction and as part of the criminal judgment, and its mandatory, offense-linked operation promotes traditional punitive aims (deterrence and retribution) even while serving compensation—features that, under Hudson’s Mendoza-Martinez purpose-and-effects factors, make it function as criminal punishment. Because the Ex Post Facto Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3) forbids laws that retroactively increase the punishment for past conduct, applying an MVRA amendment that increases restitution exposure to pre-enactment offenses triggers the Clause. Although Congress used compensatory language, the statute’s integrated placement in sentencing and its coercive enforcement mechanisms render its effects sufficiently punitive to satisfy the “clearest proof” framework discussed in Smith v. Doe and Hudson. A contrary rule would create administrability problems and statutory incoherence by allowing the Government to increase the financial consequences of a conviction retroactively simply by labeling the sanction ‘restitution.’

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, applies to criminal punishments, and under Hudson v. United States this inquiry is “at least initially, a matter of statutory construction” focused on whether Congress indicated a preference for a criminal label. The MVRA is codified in Title 18 and operates as part of the criminal judgment at sentencing, is mandatory for covered offenses, and is enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms—features that, in form and effect, align restitution with penal consequences imposed “because of” the conviction. Even if Congress invoked compensatory aims, Ward’s “clearest proof” framework supports treating MVRA restitution as punishment where it functions as a mandatory sanction tied to criminal culpability and imposed without traditional civil-law limits, so retroactive application of an MVRA change that increases exposure would increase punishment and trigger the Ex Post Facto Clause. Construing the Clause to permit retroactive increases in such mandatory sentencing consequences would erode the separation-of-powers constraint the Clause imposes on legislatures.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying the two-step intent-and-effects framework of Hudson v. United States, guided by the Mendoza-Martinez factors, MVRA restitution operates as criminal punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes because it is imposed through criminal sentencing procedures and enforced via the criminal-justice system, and it advances traditional punitive aims like deterrence and retribution. Even if Congress labeled restitution “restitution” and tied it to compensatory goals, the sanction’s practical operation—mandatory imposition upon conviction for covered offenses and integration into the criminal judgment—provides strong evidence of punitive effect when applied retroactively to increase a defendant’s exposure. Consistent with the Ex Post Facto Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3), courts should not apply an MVRA change retroactively where it increases the penalty attached to pre-enactment conduct. A clear, workable rule treating MVRA restitution as punishment for ex post facto analysis also better protects reliance interests and avoids uneven retroactive enhancements in criminal sentencing.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause forbids laws that retroactively increase “punishment,” U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, and restitution under the MVRA is imposed as part of the criminal sentence and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, features that strongly indicate a penal character notwithstanding its compensatory label. Applying the purpose-and-effects framework of Hudson v. United States and the Mendoza-Martinez factors, MVRA restitution operates only upon conviction for criminal conduct, promotes traditional punitive aims (at least deterrence and retribution), and is historically analogous to monetary penalties imposed in criminal judgments—factors that weigh toward treating it as punishment for constitutional purposes. Although restitution has a remedial aspect, the statute’s mandatory, offense-linked imposition and integration into sentencing make it difficult to maintain it is merely civil compensation, and retroactive application of an amendment that increases exposure therefore triggers ex post facto scrutiny. That conclusion is methodologically consistent with Hudson’s instruction to look past labels to the statute’s operation and effects when deciding whether a sanction is punitive.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Restitution under the MVRA is imposed “as part of” the criminal sentence, 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A(a)(1), 3572(d)(1), is mandatory for covered offenses, and is enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, all of which make its practical operation functionally punitive rather than purely remedial. Applying the Court’s intent–effects framework (Kennedy v. Mendoza-Martinez as applied in Smith v. Doe), even if Congress articulated compensatory aims, the effects of MVRA restitution—including its linkage to conviction and sentencing and its acknowledged penological purposes—are sufficiently punitive to trigger the Ex Post Facto Clause when applied retroactively to increase a defendant’s exposure. The Court’s own descriptions of restitution as a “penalty” imposed as part of a criminal sentence in Pasquantino v. United States, 544 U.S. 349, 365 (2005), and Paroline v. United States, 572 U.S. 434, 456 (2014), reinforce that characterization. Procedural fairness and reliance interests underlying Article I’s Ex Post Facto prohibition counsel against retroactive increases in such sentence-linked monetary obligations.
